claims.text: CrFeCoNiX alloys begin exposure as single-phase or multiphase metallic solid solutions.
The constituent elements are uniformly distributed before high-temperature exposure.
Preferential oxidation of X is the primary determinant of protective-scale stability and coherence above 900 °C.
Al and Si have high oxygen affinity in these CrFeCoNiX alloys.
Oxides formed from Al or Si have low oxide-growth stress.
Al- or Si-containing alloys form a continuous, nanocrystalline alumina or silica layer.
The alumina or silica layer adheres strongly to the alloy surface.
The alumina or silica layer self-heals during high-temperature exposure.
Mn initially forms discontinuous or mixed oxides in CrFeCoNiMn.
Mn-containing oxide scales are less cohesive and have higher internal stress than Al- or Si-containing scales.
The higher stress of Mn-containing oxide scales promotes cracking and spallation.
X segregates to the surface at high temperature because of its higher oxygen affinity.
An Al- or Si-rich oxide layer has low oxygen permeability and restricts further oxygen diffusion.
Al- or Si-containing alloys will undergo less continued oxidation and surface degradation than Mn-containing or X-free baselines.
Mn-containing alloys will develop unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide scales.
The proposed comparison uses Al- or Si-containing CrFeCoNiX against CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNi without X, with otherwise similar initial microstructures.
The hypothesis applies in oxidative or corrosive environments at temperatures at or above 900 °C.
Secondary phases may affect oxide-scale integrity.
Elemental diffusion kinetics may modify surface-segregation behavior.
Failure of Al- or Si-containing alloys to produce significantly more continuous and adherent scales than the controls would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and intervention specify temperatures above 900 °C, whereas the boundary includes exposure at exactly 900 °C.
